## RWX PR previews

`.rwx/preview.yml` defines the preview app (see the `rwx-reflex-preview` skill in
`.agents/skills/`). Validate with `rwx lint .rwx/preview.yml`; test with
`rwx run .rwx/preview.yml --init pull-request-number=0 --wait`. Previews are
private: access them with the `X-RWX-Access-Token` header (RWX docs). Only use
behavior documented in the RWX docs or `rwx --help`. Known open issue: the
frontend's baked-in `localhost:8000` API URL is patched in the build step
(undocumented workaround, WebSocket events unverified).

## Build & Test

```bash
uv sync --group dev          # install locked deps into .venv
uv run pytest -q             # smoke tests (`network`-marked tests deselected)
uv run tach check            # module boundaries
uv run tach check-external   # declared vs imported dependencies
trunk check --all            # lint (run uv sync first: pyright/pyrefly use .venv)
```

## Conventions

- Layers are `web.web` -> `web.pages.*` -> `web.components.*`, enforced by
  `tach.toml`; new modules need an explicit entry there.
- `tach check-external` is its own task in `.rwx/trunk-check.yml`, not a Trunk
  linter: Trunk lints from a sandbox holding only the diff, which makes every
  dependency look unused.
- `uv` ignores packages published in the last 7 days (`[tool.uv] exclude-newer`);
  pyrefly/pyright/tach pins must match between `pyproject.toml` and
  `.trunk/trunk.yaml`.
- RWX: a green run is not proof a step worked. Read task logs (`rwx logs`) for
  steps that talk to third parties.
- Use non-interactive flags (`-y`, `-f`, `trunk ... --ci < /dev/null`) in

# PR preview environment on RWX: https://www.rwx.com/blog/preview-your-web-apps-with-rwx
# Serves the exported frontend and Reflex backend through Caddy on port 3000,
# mirroring the Dockerfile/entrypoint.sh production layout.
on:
  github:
    pull_request:
      init:
        commit-sha: ${{ event.git.sha }}
        pull-request-number: ${{ event.github.pull_request.number }}
  cli:
    init:
      commit-sha: ${{ event.git.sha }}

base:
  image: ubuntu:24.04
  config: rwx/base 1.0.0

tasks:
  - key: code
    call: git/clone 2.2.0
    with:
      repository: https://github.com/elviskahoro/reflex-starter-template.git
      ref: ${{ init.commit-sha }}

  - key: system-deps
    run: |
      sudo apt-get update
      sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends caddy unzip curl
      curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
      echo "$HOME/.local/bin" >> "$RWX_ENV/PATH"

  - key: build
    use: [code, system-deps]
    run: |
      uv sync --frozen --no-dev
      .venv/bin/reflex init
      .venv/bin/reflex export --frontend-only
      sudo mkdir -p /srv
      sudo unzip -q frontend.zip -d /srv
      rm frontend.zip
      # The export bakes in http://localhost:8000; point it at the page origin
      # instead (Caddy proxies /_event and /_upload to the backend).
      f=$(grep -rl 'localhost:8000' /srv/assets | head -1)
      printf '%s\n' \
        'const o=location.origin,w=o.replace(/^http/,"ws");' \
        'var e={PING:o+"/ping",EVENT:w+"/_event",UPLOAD:o+"/_upload",AUTH_CODESPACE:o+"/auth-codespace",HEALTH:o+"/_health",ALL_ROUTES:o+"/_all_routes",TRANSPORT:"websocket",TEST_MODE:!1};export{e as t};' \
        | sudo tee "$f" > /dev/null

  - key: preview
    use: [build]
    app:
      endpoint: pr-${{ init.pull-request-number }}
      port: 3000
    run: |
      export PORT=3000 REFLEX_ENV=prod
      .venv/bin/reflex run --env prod --backend-only --backend-port 8000 &
      exec caddy run --config Caddyfile --adapter caddyfile

  - key: share-link
    use: [preview]
    run: echo "$PREVIEW_URL"
    env:
      PREVIEW_URL: ${{ tasks.preview.app.url }}

"""Smoke net for the starter template.

Builds `index_page()` so reflex's compile-time state-binding and
component plumbing run without booting the backend; the same code
`reflex export` runs in CI. status_card is exercised both via the
page factory and directly with literal inputs, plus against the
real IndexState Var shape the in-repo caller uses.

The earlier async-context test was dropped: `index_page()` is fully
synchronous, so awaiting in the test loop did not actually exercise
any async machinery. pytest-asyncio is intentionally NOT in the
dev group -- adding it back requires a real async regression, not
a placeholder.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import reflex as rx

from web.components.status_card import status_card
from web.pages.index import (
    IndexState,
    page as index_page,
)


class _TestState(rx.State):
    """Empty `rx.State` subclass used as a handler host for direct status_card tests.

    reflex accepts plain functions or coroutines for `on_click` only via
# Reflex architecture: web.web -> web.pages.index -> web.components.* (public exports only).
# rxconfig is an isolated framework entrypoint. New module imports require review.
# https://docs.gauge.sh/usage/configuration
source_roots = ["."]
root_module = "forbid"
exact = true
forbid_circular_dependencies = true
ignore_type_checking_imports = false
include_string_imports = true
# Three layers with strict ordering: production entrypoints -> pages ->
# components. Layers are NOT closed (the closed-layer flag does not
# allow per-module exemptions, and the smoke net in `tests/` needs to
# construct status_card directly with literal inputs to keep regression
# coverage honest). The intended `web.web -> web.pages.* ->
# web.components.*` flow is still enforced at the visible-edges:
# - `web.web.depends_on = ["web.pages.index"]` (entrypoint -> pages only)
# - `web.components.status_card.visibility = ["web.pages.index", "tests"]`
#   (the component is reachable from the page module and from the
#   test module, but NOT from `web.web` itself)
# - tests' visibility is `[]`, so production code cannot accidentally
#   import it.
# This is the same shape buridan-ui uses for its in-repo `tests/`
# (see .tach/trunk.yaml in that repo, which does not use `closed`).
layers = ["entrypoints", "pages", "components"]
layers_explicit_depends_on = true

# Do not let .gitignore silently remove application code from architecture checks.
respect_gitignore = false
exclude = [
  ".agents/**",
  ".claude/**",
  ".context/**",
  ".git/**",
  ".trunk/**",
  ".venv/**",
  ".web/**",
  "**/__pycache__/**",
  "symlink/**",
]

[rules]
unused_ignore_directives = "error"
require_ignore_directive_reasons = "error"
unused_external_dependencies = "error"
local_imports = "error"

[cache]
file_dependencies = [
  "tests/**",
  "pyproject.toml",
  "uv.lock",
  "tach.toml",
  "rxconfig.py",
  "reflex.lock/**",
]

# Smoke tests run pytest, which is a dev-only dep. Telling tach to skip
# external checking for pytest keeps `uv run tach check-external`
# aligned with what pyproject.toml actually declares (production deps
# only) rather than forcing pytest into `[project].dependencies`.
[external]
exclude = ["pytest"]

# Default-deny new packages instead of folding their imports into a parent module.
# Single-level globs keep each page's implementation inside its package boundary.
# Concrete module declarations below override these defaults.
[[modules]]
path = "web.*"
layer = "entrypoints"
depends_on = []
depends_on_external = []
visibility = []

[[modules]]
path = "web.pages.*"
layer = "pages"
depends_on = []
depends_on_external = []
visibility = []

[[modules]]
path = "web.components.*"
layer = "components"
depends_on = []
depends_on_external = []
visibility = []

# Reflex loads these entrypoints directly; other modules cannot import them.
[[modules]]
path = "rxconfig"
layer = "entrypoints"
depends_on = []
depends_on_external = ["reflex"]
visibility = []

[[modules]]
path = "web"
layer = "entrypoints"
depends_on = []
depends_on_external = []
visibility = []

[[modules]]
path = "web.web"
layer = "entrypoints"
depends_on = ["web.pages.index"]
depends_on_external = ["reflex"]
visibility = []

[[modules]]
path = "web.pages"
layer = "pages"
depends_on = []
depends_on_external = []
visibility = []

# Registration uses only the package's public page function.
[[modules]]
path = "web.pages.index"
layer = "pages"
depends_on = ["web.components.status_card"]
depends_on_external = ["reflex"]
# `tests` reaches this page module directly because layers are open
# (see `layers` above for why). `web.web` drives the same `page`
# symbol at runtime; the smoke net drives it at import time.
visibility = ["web.web", "tests"]

[[modules]]
path = "web.components"
layer = "components"
depends_on = []
depends_on_external = []
visibility = []

# Reusable component: takes state and handlers as arguments, imports no page.
[[modules]]
path = "web.components.status_card"
layer = "components"
depends_on = []
depends_on_external = ["reflex"]
# `tests` joins this visibility so the smoke net can call status_card
# directly with literal inputs (verifying `EventType`, `rx.Component`
# return, etc.). Production modules (`web.pages.index`) reach the
# component via the `depends_on = [...]` declaration on the page
# itself; nothing in `web.web` is allowed here because visibility
# does not list it.
visibility = ["web.pages.index", "tests"]

[[interfaces]]
# Modules have no public members unless an explicit interface below exposes them.
expose = []

[[interfaces]]
# Interface selectors are regexes, unlike module paths: escape literal dots.
from = ['web\.pages\.index']
# Both `page` (the runtime factory) and `IndexState` (the state class
# the smoke net instantiates by reference) are exposed. `page` is the
# only symbol the reflex app calls at runtime; `IndexState` is a class
# the app references by name, not by construction.
expose = ["page", "IndexState"]
# `tests` joins web.web as a permitted consumer so the smoke net can
# call the page factory and read the IndexState class at import time.
visibility = ["web.web", "tests"]
exclusive = true

[[interfaces]]
from = ['web\.components\.status_card']
expose = ["status_card"]
visibility = ["web.pages.index", "tests"]
exclusive = true

# Smoke tests are layer-peer entrypoints. They can reach
# web.pages.index and web.components.status_card directly because
# layers are open (see `layers` above). Production modules cannot
# accidentally import `tests/` because its `visibility = []` excludes
# everything from the production module graph. pytest is not in
# `depends_on_external` because [external].exclude above covers it;
# reflex is listed because every reflex page factory invocation
# imports it transitively.
[[modules]]
path = "tests"
layer = "entrypoints"
depends_on = ["web.pages.index", "web.components.status_card"]
depends_on_external = ["reflex"]
visibility = []

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

question.description: The question to ask the user

options.description: Up to 4 options for the user to choose from. Do not include 'Other' - it is automatically provided.

header.description: Short label displayed above the question.

multiSelect.description: If true, user can select multiple options. Answers are comma-separated.

content.content:
### Step 3: Commit local changes

If the pre-flight check surfaced uncommitted changes that belong in this PR, commit them **before** running roborev — roborev reviews committed history, not the working tree, so uncommitted edits would be invisible to it.

- Stage only the files that belong in this PR. Skip tool-local cruft (e.g., `.agents/`, `.claude/`, Conductor-local files) unless the user explicitly opts in.
- Commit without asking for approval: run `git commit` directly once the files are staged. The commit message should mirror the PR title's intent (sentence-cased, why-focused) — not a Conventional Commits subject. The Step 8 draft approval is still the only user-approval gate before push.
- Do **not** push yet. Push happens in Step 11, after squash, roborev, the user-confirmation gate, and the rebase.

If the working tree is already clean, skip this step.

### Step 4: Squash to a coherent set of commits

**Hard gate: squash before roborev, roborev before the user-confirmation gate, confirmation before push.** All three must happen before the branch hits `origin` so the review (and the merge) operate on the final history, not a noisy timeline.

```bash
git log main..HEAD --oneline
```

- **Default to one commit per PR.** Multi-commit PRs are only OK when each commit is independently reviewable and the slices land in order.
- Squash with `git rebase -i main` or `git reset --soft main && git commit`. Never use `--no-edit` flags that bypass message review.
- The squashed commit message mirrors the PR title's intent (sentence-cased, why-focused) and captures the motivation in the body. No Conventional Commits prefix.
- If the branch already has a single commit (or each existing commit is independently reviewable and ordered), skip the rebase but still confirm the count before moving on.
- **Never force-push to a shared branch to squash after publication.** Squash *before* the first push.

### Step 5: Run relevant tests locally, then roborev review before drafting

**Roborev reviews the diff; it does not execute the test suite.** A clean roborev pass says nothing about whether the code runs — it has caught logic/quality issues while a hardcoded assertion in a test file was still broken. Before roborev, run whatever tests cover the changed files:

- Identify affected tests by mirroring the changed path under `tests/` (many repos mirror source layout — a change to `pkg/foo.py` often has a matching `tests/.../test_foo.py`) and/or `grep -rn` the changed file's distinctive strings (a literal like an `if:` condition, a flag name) across `tests/` to catch assertions on exact values.
- Run the narrowest test target that covers the change (in a uv-based Python repo, `uv run pytest tests/<mirrored-path>`; otherwise the repo's own test command) — full-suite runs are fine too, but don't skip this step because CI will "catch it anyway": local runs take seconds, CI takes minutes.
- If a test fails, fix it now and fold the fix into the same commit (Step 3/4), *before* running roborev — don't push and let CI discover it.

**Hard gate: do not draft the PR or move toward `git push` until roborev has run and either reported clean or been explicitly acknowledged by the user.** This applies even if the change feels trivial, even if the diff is one line, and even if the user has not asked for review explicitly — the skill always runs roborev before the user is asked to approve a draft.

With the squashed commit in place but the branch still local, run a local AI code review with roborev so findings surface *before* the user sees a draft and *before* GitHub sees the diff. Invoke the `roborev` executable directly with the `--wait` flag; Git aliases are optional conveniences and may not exist in cloud sandboxes:

```bash
roborev review --wait
```

- `--wait` is **required**, not optional — it blocks until the review completes so findings are available before the draft is shown. Do not run `roborev review` without `--wait`.
- A bare `roborev review` — or a leftover post-commit auto-review hook — only **enqueues a background daemon job and returns before a verdict exists**. An enqueue is not a pass: if HEAD already has a queued or running background review, block on it (`roborev review --wait`, or `roborev wait` for the already-enqueued job) so an actual verdict is in hand before drafting. Never report "review enq
- Capture the outcome (clean, N findings fixed in M rounds, N findings unresolved, unavailable) — Step 8 surfaces it inside the draft preview so the user can see the gate was walked.
- **Review loop (no permission prompts):** if roborev surfaces findings, fix them yourself without asking — **every severity counts**, including low and nit. Do not stop, summarize, or ask "fix these?" / "defer or proceed?" because findings are low severity. Fix as many as possible that are small in scope: a wording or error-message change, a missing test case, a missing guard, a rename, a local
- **Loop cap:** stop after 3 fix rounds. If findings remain, or a finding would need a product or design decision rather than a code fix, stop looping and list the unresolved findings in the Step 8 draft preview, so the user decides at the single approval gate. Never amend or force-push past findings silently.
- If roborev is unavailable (command not installed, no network), say so explicitly to the user and ask whether to proceed without review. Do not silently skip.
- For deeper fix/refine loops, consult the repo's roborev guide skill if it ships one.

### Step 6: Draft the title

The title is a formal, sentence-cased statement of **why this change exists** — not a conventional commit subject. A reviewer scanning the PR list should understand the *motivation*, not just the area of code touched.

Rules:

- **Formal, sentence case.** "Eliminate duplicated Attio retry logic across five call sites" — not "attio retry refactor".
- **Lead with the why, not the what.** Prefer the problem solved or the outcome enabled over the mechanical change. "Unblock Linear → Attio sync from rate-limit drift" beats "Add retry decorator to Attio client".
- **No Conventional Commits prefix.** Do **not** use `feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`, `chore:`, `docs:`, etc. Even if recent commits or PRs use them, PR titles in this ecosystem are full sentences. Commit messages and PR titles are different surfaces.
- **Under 70 characters where possible**, but clarity wins over brevity — GitHub truncates in list views, so front-load the most important words.
- **Specific.** "Fix off-by-one in Apollo pagination cursor causing missed contacts" — not "Bug fix" or "Improvements".
- **No ticket IDs in the title.** They go in Links.
- **No trailing period.**
- **Avoid bare imperative verbs** like "Add", "Fix", "Update" as the first word when a why-framing is possible. They're allowed when the why genuinely is the action (e.g., a clear bugfix), but check first whether the motivation can lead instead.

Good vs. bad title shapes:

| --- | --- | --- |
| Drafting before pre-flight checks | PR opened against stale base, with uncommitted work left behind | Run the pre-flight batch first |
| Not checking for an existing PR | Duplicate PR, or `gh pr create` errors out | Always `gh pr view` first |

- **Same-repo issue, fully resolved by this PR** — the `Closes #NNN` line already lives in the PR body (Step 7's Links section). Nothing further is needed here: GitHub auto-closes the issue when the PR merges into `main`. Don't `gh issue close` it now — the fix isn't on `main` yet.
- **Cross-repo issue, or only partially resolved** — GitHub's closing keywords don't work across repos and shouldn't be used for partial work. Remember to leave a linking comment in Step 12b instead of closing it.
- **Ambiguous whether this PR fully resolves it** — this should already have been resolved in Step 2; if it wasn't, ask the user now rather than guessing at merge-closing behavior.
- Skip silently if no GitHub issue was identified in Step 2.
- Already authorized by the Step 8 "yes" — don't re-prompt.

### Step 10: Rebase onto the latest base (last step before opening the PR)

**This is the final step before the PR is opened.** Immediately before pushing, rebase the branch onto the freshest base so the PR opens against current `main` and merge conflicts surface here — locally, where they're cheap to resolve — instead of in GitHub's merge UI.

This must happen **before** the first push (Step 11), not after. Rebasing a branch that's already on `origin` would require a force-push, which is forbidden without explicit user approval.

```bash
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main   # or the confirmed base branch from pre-flight
```

- If the rebase is clean, proceed to Step 11.
- If the rebase hits conflicts, **stop and surface them to the user.** Resolve them (or have the user resolve them), then re-run Steps 4–5 (re-squash if needed, re-run `roborev review --wait`) so the review reflects the rebased history. Never `git rebase --skip` or abandon conflicting hunks silently.
- If the branch is already up to date with the base, the rebase is a no-op — proceed.

### Step 11: Push the branch

Once the rebase is clean, push the branch to `origin` with upstream tracking.

```bash
git push -u origin "$(git branch --show-current)"
```

Confirm the push succeeded before moving on. If it fails (auth, protected branch, non-fast-forward), surface the error and stop — do not force-push.

### Step 12: Create the PR

**Hard gate before running `gh pr create`: for every same-repo GitHub issue Step 2 determined this PR fully resolves, mechanically verify the drafted body contains a `Closes #NNN` / `Fixes #NNN` / `Resolves #NNN` line for *that specific* issue number before shelling out — one PR can fully resolve more than one issue, and each needs its own closing reference, not just the first.** This is a real 

```bash
grep -qiE "(closes|fixes|resolves) #${ISSUE_NUMBER}([^[:alnum:]_]|$)" <<< "$PR_BODY"
```

`\b` is not portable to the BSD `grep` on macOS — use the `([^[:alnum:]_]|$)` form above instead, which matches the same "word boundary or end of string" intent on both BSD and GNU grep.

If that grep fails for any fully-resolved issue number, **stop and fix the body** — don't proceed to `gh pr create` with a body that silently downgraded to a bare reference. If Step 2 flagged partial/cross-repo instead, the grep is expected to fail and that's correct — don't add the keyword in that case.

To make this checkable, assign the HEREDOC to `PR_BODY` first, grep that exact variable, then pass it to `--body` — don't construct the body inline in the `gh pr create` call, since there's nothing to grep before shelling out:

```bash
PR_BODY="$(cat <<'EOF'
## Why
... (real newlines, not \n)
EOF
)"

for ISSUE_NUMBER in "${FULLY_RESOLVED_ISSUE_NUMBERS[@]}"; do  # every issue Step 2 flagged as fully resolved
  grep -qiE "(closes|fixes|resolves) #${ISSUE_NUMBER}([^[:alnum:]_]|$)" <<< "$PR_BODY" || {
    echo "missing closing keyword for #${ISSUE_NUMBER}" >&2
    exit 1
  }
done

gh pr create --title "Fix race in Apollo enrichment dedup that double-charged credits" --body "$PR_BODY"
```

Return the PR URL to the user. Don't add follow-up commentary unless the user asks — the URL is the work product.

### Step 12b: Link the GitHub issue, if Step 9 deferred it

Only applies when Step 9 flagged a **cross-repo or partially-resolved** issue — the fully-resolved same-repo case already carries its `Closes #NNN` in the PR body and needs no action here.

```bash
gh issue comment <number> --body "Addressed in <PR URL from Step 12>"                    # same-repo, partial
gh issue comment <number> --repo <owner/repo> --body "Addressed in <PR URL from Step 12>" # cross-repo — use the owner/repo saved in Step 2
```

- `<PR URL>` is the output from Step 12 — this step cannot run before Step 12 for exactly that reason.
- Do not close the issue yourself; partial or cross-repo work isn't the maintainer's signal to close it.
- Skip silently if Step 9 found nothing to do here.

### Step 13: Suggest the merge once tests and checks pass

Merging is never automatic. Once the PR is open, check its status with a single call (`gh pr checks <pr-number>`). When tests and required checks have passed, suggest merging with the GitHub CLI and wait for the user to say yes:

```bash
gh pr merge <pr-number> --squash
```

- Do not poll in a loop. If checks are still running, report that and stop; the user can ask again later.
- Do not log in to, configure, or call any merge-queue service. If `gh` is not authenticated, say so and stop.
- Never pass `--admin` or `--auto` unless the user asks for it.

## Modifiers: drafts, reviewers, labels

`gh pr create` accepts modifiers that don't affect the description but matter for the PR's lifecycle. Don't auto-set any of these; only pass what the user explicitly asks for:

| Flag | When |
| --- | --- |
| `--draft` | User says "draft", or commit history shows clear in-progress markers ("WIP", "spike"). |
| `--reviewer <handle>` | Only when the user names reviewers. Don't guess. |
| `--label <name>` | Only labels that exist (`gh label list`). Invented labels silently no-op. |
| `--assignee <handle>` | Default to `@me` unless told otherwise. |
| `--base <branch>` | Only override the default branch when the user says so. |

## Anti-patterns

These show up in autogenerated PR descriptions and this skill must actively avoid them. Several come from defaults baked into other tools — including the default `gh pr create` template suggested by the Bash tool — and this skill overrides them.

### Don't summarize the diff

```markdown
## Summary
- Added `retry_with_backoff` helper in `apollo/client.py`
- Updated `enrich_account` to use it
- Added 3 unit tests in `test_apollo.py`
```

The reviewer is about to read the diff. This is duplicate work that rots the moment the diff changes. Replace with **Why**.

### Don't write empty sections

```markdown
## Risks
None.

## Test plan
Tested locally.
```

"None" and "Tested locally" carry zero signal. Drop the section.

### Don't add AI attribution

The repo's agent instructions (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md) prohibit AI attribution in commits and PRs.
**Never** emit:

- `Co-Authored-By: Claude <claude@anthropic.com>`
- `🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](...)`
- Any "Generated by ..." or "Powered by ..." footer

The Bash tool's default PR template includes the 🤖 footer. **Strip it.** This skill overrides that default.

### Don't restate the title

If the title is "Fix race in Apollo enrichment dedup", the description shouldn't open with "This PR fixes a race in the Apollo enrichment dedup logic." Start the Why with the problem, not a rephrase.

### Don't pad with boilerplate

- "This PR makes some improvements to ..."
- "As discussed offline, ..."
- "Cleaning up some technical debt ..."

If you can't write a specific Why, pause and ask the user. Vague motivation is a tell that the work isn't ready for review.

### Don't paste test output

The Test plan section is about the *reasoning* behind what was tested. A reviewer can run the tests. They cannot rederive your reasoning from the output.

### Don't include "Closes #NNN" without confirming

GitHub auto-closes referenced issues on merge. Only use `Closes` / `Fixes` / `Resolves` keywords if Step 2 confirmed the PR fully resolves a **same-repo** issue. For partial work or a cross-repo issue, mention it in Links instead and leave a linking comment on the issue in Step 12b — no magic keyword. Skipping the confirmation in Step 2 is a bug, not a safe default: it leaves the issue open with

### Don't autopilot the PR submission

Even if the user said "create a PR for this", they agreed to the action, not to a specific draft. Show the draft, wait for confirmation, then submit.

## Examples

### Example 1: Small bug fix — Why + Links only

**Title:** `Fix off-by-one in Apollo pagination cursor causing missed contacts`

**Body:**

```markdown
## Why
The Apollo `search_people` paginator was dropping the last page of results because the cursor check used `>` instead of `>=`. Affected every batch where total results were an exact multiple of page_size — roughly 10% of runs. Caught when a TAM build was missing ~50 known contacts ([AI-1234](https://linear.app/...)).

## Links
- Linear: [AI-1234](https://linear.app/...)
```

(Trade-offs, Risks, Test plan dropped — small obvious fix, full coverage exists.)

### Example 2: Refactor — Why + Trade-offs + Risks + Links

**Title:** `Consolidate Attio retry logic to unblock Linear → Attio sync`

**Body:**

```markdown
## Why
Five call sites in `libs/attio/` were duplicating retry/backoff logic, and each had drifted: `update_person` retried on 5xx but not 429; `create_person` retried on 429 but with no backoff; `list_workspaces` did no retry at all. The new Linear → Attio sync was about to become the sixth divergent copy.

Pulling the logic into `@retry_with_backoff` lets callers opt in with one line and ensures consistent behavior across all Attio writes.

## Trade-offs
Considered `tenacity` instead. Rejected because the call sites already have idiosyncratic logic — custom backoff that respects Attio's `Retry-After` header — that `tenacity` would require a custom wait strategy to express. The hand-rolled decorator is ~30 lines and stays close to the Attio-specific behavior.

## Risks
Changes the *shape* of exceptions that bubble up: `AttioRateLimit` is now wrapped in `RetryExhausted` after N attempts. Two existing callers caught `AttioRateLimit` directly; both updated in this PR. Grep for `AttioRateLimit` returns no other matches.

## Links
- Linear: [AI-2891](https://linear.app/...)
- Spec: design/backlog-202604010000-attio_retry_decorator-spec-01.md
```

### Example 3: Bad → Good

**Bad:**

```markdown
## Summary
- Added retry decorator
- Updated 5 Attio call sites
- Removed duplicate retry code
- Added tests

## Test plan
- [x] Ran tests
- [x] Tested locally

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
```

What's wrong: the Summary paraphrases the diff, the Test plan has no reasoning, the AI footer is forbidden, and there's no motivation a reviewer can use to evaluate the change.

**Good:** see Example 2.

## Failure modes and recovery

| What happened | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Linear MCP unavailable or ticket not found | Continue without the Linear context. Note in Links: "Linear ticket: AI-NNN (MCP unavailable at draft time)" and let the user fill in. |
| Branch doesn't match a Linear pattern | Skip the Linear lookup. Rely on design artifacts and conversation. |
| No design artifact, no ticket, no clear Why from the conversation | Stop. Ask the user: "I can't establish a specific Why for this PR from the available context. Can you summarize the motivation in 1-2 sentences?" |
| `gh pr create` fails (auth, network, no remote) | Surface the error to the user. Don't retry without diagnosing. |
| User rejects the draft | Take their feedback and rewrite. Don't argue. |
| User wants to skip the confirmation step | Honor it — but require an explicit "skip confirmation" or "just create it" from them. Default is to confirm. |

## Common pitfalls

| Pitfall | Why it bites | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drafting before pre-flight checks | PR opened against stale base, with uncommitted work left behind | Run the pre-flight batch first |
| Not checking for an existing PR | Duplicate PR, or `gh pr create` errors out | Always `gh pr view` first |
| Pasting the Linear ticket verbatim | Description becomes a wall of duplicated text | Paraphrase the problem statement; link the rest |
| Filling all sections regardless of signal | Skim-defeating filler | Drop sections that don't carry meaning |
| Autopiloting `gh pr create` | Premature publication; harder to retract than to delay | Show draft, wait for confirmation |
| Inheriting the default 🤖 footer | Violates the repo's no-AI-attribution rule | Strip it from the body |
| Trusting a clean roborev as proof the code runs | Roborev reviews the diff, not test execution — a hardcoded test assertion (e.g. a literal YAML `if:` string) can still fail in CI | Run the mirrored test file / grep for affected literals before roborev (Step 5) |
| Using "WIP" in title instead of `--draft` | Title noise; doesn't actually mark the PR as draft | Use `gh pr create --draft` and a clean title |
| Linking to the PR's own branch name as "context" | The branch is implicit; this is noise | Only link to artifacts that aren't already obvious from the PR |
| Forgetting the linked GitHub issue entirely | Issue lingers open after merge with no trace back to the PR that fixed it | Resolve it in Step 2, `Closes #NNN` in Step 7, record disposition in Step 9, comment in Step 12b |
| Drafting `Closes #NNN` in Step 7 but the final body sent to `gh pr create` drops it (edits, re-drafts, template drift) | Issue never auto-closes even though Step 2/9 correctly flagged full resolution — happened for real on gtm-sdk#609/#628 | Step 12's mechanical grep gate on the literal `--body` string, not on what Step 7 intended to write |

## Red flags (stop and rethink)

- **About to `git push` without running `roborev review --wait` first.** This is the repository-wide roborev gate defined in the repo's agent instructions; no PR should skip it.
- **About to `git push` with more commits than the PR needs.** Squash to a coherent set first (Step 4); don't rely on GitHub's "Squash and merge" button to clean up history before review.
- Drafting a PR with no Linear ticket, no design artifact, and no conversation-derived motivation.
- Writing more than 3 paragraphs in Why. If you need that much, the work is probably two PRs.
- Including a `## Summary` section. This is the default template's tell — replace with `## Why`.
- Including a 🤖 footer.
- More than 5 bullets in any one section. Each bullet should be load-bearing.
